Q: How does the lead capture tool work?

<source id="1" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/knowledge-base/" title="Knowledge Base" section="FAQ Knowledge Source > How FAQ Matching Works">
Knowledge Base > FAQ Knowledge Source > How FAQ Matching Works

1. User's query is tokenized into words
2. Each FAQ pair is scored by word frequency overlap (question + answer)
3. Top 5 matching FAQs are returned as context
4. Context is formatted as `Q: ...\nA: ...` and injected into the AI prompt
</source>
<source id="2" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/knowledge-base/" title="Knowledge Base" section="FAQ Knowledge Source">

```typescript
import { FAQKnowledgeSource } from '@chatcops/core';

const faq = new FAQKnowledgeSource([
  { question: 'What are your business hours?', answer: '9am-5pm EST, Monday to Friday.' },
  { question: 'Do you offer refunds?', answer: 'Yes, full refunds within 30 days.' },
  { question: 'How do I contact support?', answer: 'Email support@example.com or use this chat!' },
  { question: 'What payment methods do you accept?', answer: 'Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, and wire transfer.' },
]);
```
</source>
<source id="3" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/knowledge-base/" title="Knowledge Base" section="Text Knowledge Source > How Text Matching Works">
Knowledge Base > Text Knowledge Source > How Text Matching Works

1. Each string in the array is one chunk
2. User's query words are matched against each chunk
3. Top 3 relevant chunks are returned
4. Context is prefixed with `"Relevant context:\n"`
</source>
<source id="4" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/knowledge-base/" title="Knowledge Base" section="KnowledgeSource Interface">
Knowledge Base > KnowledgeSource Interface

```typescript
import type { RetrievalQuery, RetrievedChunk } from '@chatcops/core';

interface KnowledgeSource {
  type: string;
  getContext(query: string): Promise<string>;
  // Optional: the matching chunks themselves, with the conversation so far.
  retrieve?(query: RetrievalQuery): Promise<RetrievedChunk[]>;
}
```

When a source has `retrieve`, the server uses it instead of `getContext`. It passes the visitor's message and the last few messages before it, so a follow-up like "how long does it take?" can be searched in context. The chunks from every source are numbered and given to the model in one fenced block, marked as reference material that never contains instructions, since crawled pages sometimes do. That's what citations will build on.
</source>
<source id="5" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/knowledge-base/" title="Knowledge Base" section="Retrieval from a vector store">
Knowledge Base > Retrieval from a vector store

The newer Voyage models (`voyage-4`, `voyage-4-lite`, `voyage-3.5` and others) can shorten their vectors with `dimensions` (256, 512, 1024 or 2048). Other models make one fixed length, so set `dimensions` to that length. `batchSize` is how many texts go in one request (128 by default, at most 1,000); each model also limits the tokens in a request, so lower it for very long texts.

In a Cloudflare Worker, pass the `AI` binding directly:

```typescript
import {
  memoryVectors,
  retrieverKnowledge,
  vectorRetriever,
  workersAiEmbedder,
  workersAiReranker,
  type WorkersAiBinding,
} from '@chatcops/core';

declare const env: { AI: WorkersAiBinding };

const embedder = workersAiEmbedder({ ai: env.AI });
const vectors = memoryVectors({ dimensions: embedder.dimensions });
const reranker = workersAiReranker({ ai: env.AI });
const knowledge = retrieverKnowledge(vectorRetriever({ store: vectors, embedder, reranker }), { topK: 5 });
```

There are two retrievers:

| Retriever | Searches by | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| `vectorRetriever({ store, embedder })` | Meaning: the question is embedded and compared with every chunk | Any vector store |
| `hybridRetriever({ store, embedder })` | Meaning and exact words, merged by rank (reciprocal rank fusion, `rrfK` 60) | A store with `keywordQuery` |

Hybrid search is the better default when the store supports it. Words catch what meaning misses, such as product names, error codes and part numbers.

Both take `candidates` (how many records each search fetches, default 20) and an optional `reranker`, which reorders the candidates before the top ones are kept. A short follow-up question ("how long does it take?") is searched together with the visitor's previous question, so it finds the right pages.
</source>
</sources>

<source id="1" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/knowledge-base/" title="Knowledge Base" section="Building an index from your site">
Knowledge Base > Building an index from your site

`@chatcops/ingest` fills a vector store from your site: it reads your sitemap (or a list of URLs, or a folder of Markdown and HTML files), extracts each page's readable content, splits it into chunks along headings, and embeds them.

```typescript
import { memoryStorage, memoryVectors, openaiEmbedder } from '@chatcops/core';
import { ingest } from '@chatcops/ingest';

const embedder = openaiEmbedder({ apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY! });
const storage = memoryStorage();
const vectors = memoryVectors({ dimensions: embedder.dimensions });

const stats = await ingest({
  sources: [{ type: 'sitemap', url: 'https://example.com/sitemap.xml' }],
  exclude: ['**/blog/**'],
  embedder,
  store: vectors,
  manifest: storage.kv!,
});
```

In production, use a persistent vector store and its key-value store as the `manifest`. Running it again then only embeds pages that changed: unchanged pages answer `304` to a conditional request, or extract to the same text. Hidden elements, scripts, styles and comments are removed before extraction. `prune: true` removes pages that are gone, but never after a sitemap failed to load. An index remembers which embedder built it and refuses a different one.

Network sources respect `robots.txt` by default, using the `ChatCopsBot` group or falling back to `*`. Disallowed pages are skipped with the reason `blocked by robots.txt`. Policies are fetched once per origin per run, and `crawl-delay` sets the minimum interval between requests to that origin. A 4xx response permits crawling; a 5xx response or unreachable robots server blocks it. Up to five redirects are followed. Set `respectRobots: false` in the ingest config to opt out. Directory sources read local files and are never checked.
</source>

|---|---|

| `{ type: 'urls', urls }` | The pages you list |
| `{ type: 'directory', path, baseUrl }` | Local `.md`, `.mdx` and `.html` files, cited as if published under `baseUrl` |

Testing your bot > Judged by a model

Some things a reply should do don't fit in a `contains`: "confirms the demo without inventing a meeting time", "apologizes once and doesn't argue". A `judge` assertion has a second model grade the reply against a rubric:

```yaml
expect:
  - judge: "Confirms the demo request without inventing a meeting time."
  - judge: { rubric: "Apologizes once and doesn't argue.", threshold: 0.8 }
```

The judge sees the rubric and the conversation so far, scores the last reply from 0 to 1, and gives a reason. The assertion passes at `threshold` or above (0.7 when you don't set one), and a failure prints the score and the reason.

By default the judge is the cheap model of a different provider than your bot's: Gemini's default model, or OpenAI's when the bot runs on Gemini. A model grading its own answers tends to score them too kindly. Its key comes from `GEMINI_API_KEY` (or `GOOGLE_API_KEY`), `OPENAI_API_KEY` or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, and without one the run stops before it starts instead of skipping the judged tests.
```ts
import { defineConfig } from '@chatcops/cli';

export default defineConfig({
  server: { provider: { type: 'claude', apiKey: process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY! }, systemPrompt: 'You answer questions about Acme.' },
  judge: { type: 'openai', apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY!, model: 'gpt-5-mini' },
});
```

<source id="1" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/tools/" title="Tools" section="How Tools Work">
Tools > How Tools Work

1. The AI decides when to call a tool based on conversation context
2. ChatCops converts tool definitions to the provider's native format
3. When the AI invokes a tool, `execute()` runs server-side
4. The result is fed back to the AI, which formulates a response
5. Visitors only see the final message. The tool calls and their results are saved with it, so the next reply knows what the tools returned.

All the calls the model makes in one step run at the same time. A tool that takes longer than `toolTimeoutMs` (default 30 seconds) gets an error result, and its `signal` aborts.

When a tool throws, the model only hears `Tool failed: <name>`. What a tool throws can hold anything, such as a database error with a connection string, and the model could repeat it to the visitor. The full error goes to the server's [logger](/server/setup/#logging) as a `tool_error`. To tell the model something it can pass on, return a failure instead of throwing:

```typescript
import type { ToolResult } from '@chatcops/core';

declare function findOrder(id: string): Promise<{ status: string } | undefined>;

async function lookupOrder(id: string): Promise<ToolResult> {
  const order = await findOrder(id);
  if (!order) return { success: false, message: `There's no order ${id}. Ask the visitor to check the number.` };
  return { success: true, data: order };
}
```

Tools get the server's logger as `context.logger` too, for problems they handle themselves.

Always the first event in a successful stream:

```json
{
  "type": "start",
  "protocol": 1,
  "conversationId": "c_8f2",
  "messageId": "m_91a0c4",
  "capabilities": {
    "session": true
  }
}
```

Surrounds and streams chunks of assistant text:

```json
{ "type": "text-start", "id": "t1" }
```

```json
{ "type": "text-delta", "id": "t1", "delta": "Hello! How can I help you today?" }
```

```json
{ "type": "text-end", "id": "t1" }
```

Sent when a `knowledge` source has `retrieve()` and the reply cites a chunk from it, at most once per page. `sourceId` is the page's `source.id`, and `snippet` is the chunk's text with whitespace collapsed, cut to 200 characters.   "sourceId": "src_faq_1",

```json
  "snippet": "Our Starter plan begins at $19/mo."
}
```

```json
  "type": "tool-result",
  "toolCallId": "call_123",
  "output": { "status": "shipped", "tracking": "TRK987654" }
}
```

Emitted when visitor contact details are captured:

```json
{
  "type": "lead-captured",
  "lead": {
    "name": "Jane Doe",
    "email": "jane@example.com",
    "projectDetails": "Need custom chatbot integration"
  }
}
```

```yaml
name: Orders
defaults:

  mocks:
    tools:

tests:

    repeat: 5
    passRate: 0.8
    turns:
```

<source id="4" url="https://chat.codercops.com/core/testing/" title="Testing your bot" section="Eval files">

Server Setup > Budgets

Budgets cap what replies can cost, so a script hammering your endpoint can't run up the bill. They're counted in `storage`, so they hold across instances.

They're on by default:

| Scope | Default | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `perConversation` | 200 replies | The widget keeps a conversation across visits, so this counts replies rather than tokens, which would grow with the size of your system prompt. |
| `perIpPerDay` | 2M tokens | The cost backstop. A script can start new conversations at will, but not new IPs as easily. |
| `globalPerDay` | none | No single number fits every site. Set one. |

The server logs the budgets in force once at startup:


```typescript
import type { ChatCopsServerConfig } from '@chatcops/server';

const config: Partial<ChatCopsServerConfig> = {
  budgets: {
    perConversation: { tokens: 400_000 },            // over the conversation's lifetime
    perIpPerDay: { tokens: 2_000_000, messages: 200 },
    globalPerDay: { usd: 20 },                        // the backstop
    // What a request cost, for the dollar cap. Price cached input at its discount.

};
```

```yaml
        expect:
          - contains: "$19"
```

```typescript
    perIpPerDay: { tokens: 2_000_000, messages: 200 },
```

The Upstash store uses an existing dense index configured for cosine distance. Set its dimensions to match your embedder. The store preserves the page source in reserved metadata fields, so `deleteBySource()` can remove all of a page's chunks. Configure a dedicated test index with at least four dimensions to run conformance; tests do not reset the index.

```bash
npm install @chatcops/store-upstash-vector @upstash/vector
```

```typescript
import { memoryStorage } from '@chatcops/core';
import { Index } from '@upstash/vector';
import { upstashVectors } from '@chatcops/store-upstash-vector';

const dimensions = 1024;
const index = new Index({
  url: process.env.UPSTASH_VECTOR_REST_URL!,
  token: process.env.UPSTASH_VECTOR_REST_TOKEN!,
});
const storage = {
  ...memoryStorage(),
  vectors: upstashVectors({ index, dimensions }),
};
```

Metadata filters require every key to match and accept any value in an array. For sparse indexes and hybrid indexes with a sparse text embedding model, pass `keywordSearch: true` to expose `keywordQuery`. Dense indexes leave that method absent. The SDK does not encode the configured index kind in its `Index` type, so only enable this option for supported indexes.

Storage

The server uses storage for conversation history and, when the configured store provides the capability, counters, turn locks, and analytics events.

By default, conversations are kept in memory for one server process. The memory store holds up to 1000 conversations, evicting the least recently used first, and drops conversations that have been idle for 7 days. That is useful for local development, but it is not reliable for Vercel, Lambda, Workers, or any multi-instance deployment: instances do not share memory, and a restart removes the data.   maxConversations: 5000,                  // default 1000, least recently used dropped first
```typescript
  conversationTtlMs: 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000,  // default 7 days idle

  maxEvents: 50_000,                        // analytics events, default 10,000, oldest dropped first
});
```

Past `maxKeys`, expired counters and keys are swept first, and only then are the oldest dropped.

<source id="1" url="https://chat.codercops.com/widget/pre-chat-form/" title="Pre-chat Form">
Pre-chat Form

The pre-chat form collects information such as a visitor's name, email, or reason for contacting you before the conversation begins. Configure it in JavaScript with `ChatCops.init()`:

```typescript
import ChatCops from '@chatcops/widget';

ChatCops.init({
  apiUrl: 'https://your-api.com/chat',
  preChatForm: {
    enabled: true,
    title: 'Before we start...',
    subtitle: 'Tell us a bit about yourself',
    submitLabel: 'Start chat',
    fields: [
      { name: 'name', type: 'text', label: 'Name', placeholder: 'Your name', required: true },
      { name: 'email', type: 'email', label: 'Email', placeholder: 'you@example.com' },
      {
        name: 'topic',
        type: 'select',
        label: 'What can we help with?',
        options: ['Sales', 'Support', 'Billing'],
      },
      { name: 'message', type: 'textarea', label: 'Message', placeholder: 'How can we help?' },
    ],
  },
  onPreChatSubmit(data) {
    console.log('Pre-chat answers:', data);
  },
});
```

The form appears when there is no saved conversation with messages and the visitor has not already submitted the form for the saved conversation. The answers are kept with the conversation, so they last as long as it does (see [saved conversations](/widget/configuration/#saved-conversations)). After submission, the widget switches to the chat view. If a field is named `name`, its answer personalizes the welcome message. If a field is named `message`, its answer is sent as the conversation's first chat message immediately after submission.
</source>
<source id="2" url="https://chat.codercops.com/widget/pre-chat-form/" title="Pre-chat Form" section="Form options > Field options">
Pre-chat Form > Form options > Field options

| Option | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `string` | Required key for the answer. Use `name` to personalize the welcome message or `message` to start the chat with the visitor's answer. |
| `type` | `'text' \| 'email' \| 'select' \| 'textarea'` | Required input type. Email fields are checked for a valid email format. |
| `label` | `string` | Required text label displayed above the field. |
| `placeholder` | `string` | Optional placeholder. For a select, this replaces the default prompt. If omitted, the select prompt comes from `strings.selectPlaceholder` (English default: `Select {label}...`). |
| `required` | `boolean` | Optional. When `true`, the visitor must enter or select a non-empty value before submitting. Defaults to `false`. |
| `options` | `string[]` | Optional choices for a `select` field. |

Required fields are checked for non-empty values, and non-empty `email` fields are checked for email format. Invalid fields show an error and the form stays open until corrected. Values are trimmed before they are submitted.
</source>

Tell the widget who the signed-in visitor is.

- `token` is the identity token for [signed-in visitors](/server/setup/#signed-in-visitors), which your server signs.
- `name` and `email` are sent to the bot as visitor details with the first message of a conversation, and the name greets them.

Switching to another user, or `setUser(null)` when the visitor signs out, clears the chat, so one person's conversation never shows for the next. With the script tag build, a call before the chat has loaded is kept until it does.

```typescript
ChatCops.setUser({ name: session.name, email: session.email, token: session.chatToken });

// When the visitor signs out:

```

Use `onPreChatSubmit` in the widget config to receive the submitted answers in your application:

```typescript
const analytics = { track: (_event: string, _data: Record<string, string>) => {} };
ChatCops.init({
  apiUrl: 'https://your-api.com/chat',
  preChatForm: { enabled: true, fields: [{ name: 'email', type: 'email', label: 'Email' }] },

  },
});
```

```typescript
ChatCops.on('preChatSubmit', (data) => {

});
```

Theming > Light, dark and auto > Upgrading from a dark-only version

Earlier versions of the widget were always dark. Now it's light on light systems, which suits most sites better. To keep the old look everywhere, set `mode: 'dark'` (or `data-theme-mode="dark"`).

If your config sets `bgColor` or `textColor` and no `mode`, the widget picks the mode those colors were made for: a dark `bgColor` or a light `textColor` means dark, so a custom dark theme keeps working as it was.
</source>

Theming > Light, dark and auto

The widget has a light and a dark look. By default (`mode: 'auto'`) it follows the visitor's system setting, and switches while the page is open when that setting changes. Pin one with `mode`:

```typescript
ChatCops.init({
  apiUrl: '/api/chat',
  theme: {
    mode: 'light',               // 'light', 'dark' or 'auto' (the default)
    accent: '#4f46e5',           // buttons, the launcher, visitor messages
    accentDark: '#a5b4fc',       // the accent in dark mode; defaults to accent
    fontFamily: 'Inter, sans-serif',
    borderRadius: 12,            // px if a number, or any CSS length like '1rem'
    position: 'bottom-right',    // or 'bottom-left'
  },
});
```

On the script tag, these are `data-theme-mode`, `data-accent` and `data-accent-dark`.

| Element | Light | Dark |
|---------|-------|------|
| Background | `#ffffff` | `#0a0a0a` |
| Surface (bot messages, header) | `#f4f5f7` | `#1a1a1a` |
| Input area | `#ffffff` | `#2a2a2a` |
| Border | `#d9dce1` | `#333333` |
| Text | `#1a1d23` | `#ffffff` |
| Secondary text | `#5b616e` | `#a0a0a0` |
| Accent | `#4f46e5` | `#6366f1` |
| Errors | `#c62828` | `#ef4444` |

The dark look is the one the widget had before light mode existed. Text on the accent is picked for contrast (white or near-black, with the accent darkened a little when neither reaches 4.5:1), in each mode for its own accent.
</source>
<source id="3" url="https://chat.codercops.com/widget/theming/" title="Theming" section="ThemeConfig Interface">
Theming > ThemeConfig Interface

```typescript
interface ThemeConfig {
  mode?: 'light' | 'dark' | 'auto';  // Default 'auto': follows the system setting
  accent?: string;          // Hex color
  accentDark?: string;      // Hex color, the accent in dark mode. Defaults to accent
  textColor?: string;       // Hex color
  bgColor?: string;         // Hex color
  fontFamily?: string;      // CSS font-family string
  borderRadius?: string | number;  // px if a number or numeric string (12, '12'), or any CSS length ('1rem')
  position?: 'bottom-right' | 'bottom-left';
}
```
</source>
<source id="4" url="https://chat.codercops.com/widget/configuration/" title="Widget Configuration" section="Programmatic Configuration > Popup Mode">
Widget Configuration > Programmatic Configuration > Popup Mode

```typescript
import ChatCops from '@chatcops/widget';

ChatCops.init({
  apiUrl: 'https://your-api.com/chat',
  timeout: 60000, // Abort after 60s without received data (default: 30000ms)

  // Theme
  theme: {
    mode: 'auto',               // 'light' | 'dark' | 'auto' (follows the system)
    accent: '#4f46e5',
    accentDark: '#a5b4fc',      // optional accent for dark mode
    fontFamily: 'Inter, sans-serif',
    borderRadius: '12',
    position: 'bottom-right',   // 'bottom-right' | 'bottom-left'
  },

  // Branding
  branding: {
    name: 'Support Bot',
    avatar: 'https://example.com/avatar.png',
    subtitle: 'Usually replies instantly',
  },

  // Behavior
  welcomeMessage: 'Hi! How can I help you today?',
  suggestions: ['Compare plans', 'Book a demo'],
  welcomeBubble: {
    text: 'Need help? Chat with us!',
    delay: 3000,
  },
  placeholder: 'Type a message...',
  autoOpen: 1000,  // Open after 1s, or true for immediate
  locale: 'en',
});
```
